title: EchoMotion tracks full body with a single smartwatch
excerpt: Cornell researchers use ultrasonic sound and a tiny AI model on a smartwatch to capture whole-body pose with under-four-inch error.
body:
A Cornell research team demonstrated that a single commercial smartwatch can act like a sonar scanner for the whole body. By sending ultrasonic pulses from the watch’s speaker and listening to the echoes with its microphone, the device builds a 3-D pose map without any cameras. The proof-of-concept ran on an off-the-shelf Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 and achieved joint-position errors under four inches for users who had never seen the system before.

The study also showed that the method works in a small room, a narrow hallway, and even next to a noisy road, while consuming only a fraction of the battery that a wearable camera would need. The following sections explain how the technology works, what accuracy it achieved, and why the approach is both power-efficient and privacy-preserving.

## EchoMotion turns a smartwatch into an active acoustic sensor  

EchoMotion uses the built-in speaker and microphone on a commercial smartwatch as a tiny sonar system. Two speakers emit short bursts of ultrasonic sound that are inaudible to humans. The bursts spread outward in a sphere around the wearer. When the pulses hit a limb, part of the energy bounces back and is captured by the microphones.  

A lightweight deep-learning model then translates the pattern of echoes into the positions of 12 key joints, from head to ankles. Because the system relies only on sound, it does not need line-of-sight and is not confused by furniture or ambient light. The researchers tested the system in three environments, a quiet room, a narrow hallway, and beside a busy road, and found that neither furniture nor background noise disrupted the echo measurements.

## Building and training the model  

The team first created a 3-D-printed watch replica that held a speaker-mic pair on each side. Ten volunteers wore the prototype on their nondominant hand while performing 18 different exercises. The prototype recorded the ultrasonic echoes and a set of reference camera captures. Using those paired data, the researchers trained a deep-learning model to map echo signatures to joint locations.  

After training, the model was deployed on an unmodified Samsung Galaxy Watch 6. Fifteen new volunteers tried the system without any hardware changes. The average error for predicting each joint’s position was under four inches.

A single 12-minute calibration session reduced the error to about 2.4 inches, a drop of more than one third. The same model also ran on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3 without any retraining, showing that the approach scales across different commercial devices.

## Power use and privacy advantages  

EchoMotion’s acoustic sensing stage draws roughly 12 mW, which is about 40 times less than the power required by a typical wearable camera. In a 30-minute tracking session on the Galaxy Watch 6, only 5 %, 6 % of the battery was consumed.  

Because the system never captures visual data, it preserves privacy for both the wearer and anyone nearby. The data stream consists of short echo recordings, which are far smaller than video frames. This makes on-device processing cheaper and easier to secure, and it eliminates the need for users to worry about cameras in gyms or therapy rooms.

## Potential applications  

When integrated into commercial wearables or virtual-reality headsets, EchoMotion could support a range of use cases:

- Tracking workouts and providing real-time feedback on form.  
- Monitoring daily activities for health-span studies.  
- Guiding physical-rehabilitation exercises with automatic pose verification.  

The authors note that the technology offers a scalable way for AI to understand human behavior in real-world settings, without the cost and privacy concerns of camera-based systems.

## The takeaway  

A single smartwatch can provide full-body pose tracking by emitting and listening to ultrasonic sound. The approach delivers sub-four-inch joint accuracy on unmodified devices, cuts power use dramatically, and avoids visual privacy concerns. For developers, the key is to use the watch’s existing speaker-mic pair with a small AI model, no extra hardware, no camera, and minimal battery impact.  

*Source: [Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/11/researchers-track-whole-body-movement-just-smartwatch).*
